utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused are here. The parties' composition is exactly the same as yesterday and the day before. So the witness is here. Witness, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony and hopefully conclude it soon. You are testifying to your solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth. Mr. Bourgon had finished, Mr. Zivanovic has finished. Who was planned to go next? Mr. Lazarevic

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, dobro jutro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. In the statement given to the OTP you state that at the same location, and we won't mention the name, the same location that were you at, that there was a state security unit as well. You said that that unit was established at a later stage, once you had already arrived there in mid-1995. Do you remember that part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You also state that your unit exchanged information with that state security unit; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to clarify this exchange of information for us. Was it a two-way exchange, meaning you provided your information to them and the other way around, or was it only a one-way exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always exchanged frequencies. That was the most common thing we exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How about the conversations you intercepted and transcribed, did you compare them to the ones intercepted by the state security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, what sort of relationship did you have with the members of state security who worked at the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can I ask, can we move for just a little while on the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The platoon commander we have just mentioned was present there and supervised your work; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you had regular, daily contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was your relationship with him a good one, as would be between two good colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At a certain point in 1995 was there a certain incident involving the commander of your platoon and a member of the state security at the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did your platoon commander complain to you saying that some members of the state security committed a criminal report against him, because of the fact that he destroyed some equipment, believing it interfered with the work of your station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us turn to another topic. The topic of the notebooks you mentioned, and in -- which the intercepts were transcribed into. Did you have those notebooks all the time, or did you occasionally transcribe a certain conversation on a sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we always used notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Another question in relation to that. At the location you were at were there any files of the main participants in the intercepts which would contain the features of their accept, characteristic words they would use, their nicknames or similar, alongside with their name, rank and function within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you've never seen such a thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, at this point, I would have to ask for the assistance of my colleagues from the Prosecution and the assistance of Madam Usher. I would like the witness to take a look at notebook number 26 which is already tendered here into documents. And if the witness could be shown the page with ERN number 718633. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you identified your handwriting in this conversation beginning after 255. I'm interested in the two lines just before that at the top of the page. Is that your handwriting as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we take a look at the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this your handwriting as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at, I believe it to be the sixth and the 7th line on the page stating why. Who is the signals man Z, says -- I can't make it out clearly, but you think it says, "This is" or "here is a guy by the name of Borovcanin? Can you tell me whether this is indeed what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you say you transcribed that conversation from the tape, and you were the one who intercepted it, judging by the fact that this is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we go back, or rather go one page back at the top? [In English] The other one. This is the next page. The previous page. Oh, yes, that's the one. [Interpretation] At the top of the page in the top left-hand corner there is a word, "Borovcanin." Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you identified that person to be a radio man or a signals man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To sum up, you say you intercepted a conversation in which one of the participants was Borovcanin, and that you identified him as a signals man. Is that a fair interpretation of everything we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what I wrote down, it should be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Hvala lepo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement you spoke of the channels on the -- where the reels were not always sent, you wanted to re-use them, they were not always sent. I would like to know when you re-used those reels, did you record directly on them or would you erase them first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation was not very clear. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were reusing the reels, the tapes on we you already are conversations taped, did you erase those tapes or did you tape directly the new conversation on the former one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always used new tapes. We would send them down to the command and would receive them back erased, blank.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2345, the statement to the Prosecutor's office. Sir, could you look at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you like this, but we seem to have a problem. We -- at least I and my colleagues definitely cannot -- do not have on the monitor the document. I don't know if the rest of you have it or not. But obviously you're referring the witness to this document. If he can't see it, we have to -- he can see it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness can see the document, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come? Oh, I see. I see. All right. Yeah, go ahead. We'll follow from the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, page 3, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I want to make sure that we can follow, because we've got hard copies. You can follow because you probably have hard copies as well, but your clients don't. So we'll only proceed if you agree that we can proceed. Is there any one of you that objects with us proceeding, or do you want to wait until this comes up on the screen? We can solve it very easily, we can put it on the ELMO and then everyone can follow. I take it that there is no objection? Yes, Madam Fauveau, if you can proceed that and if you can dig it up and put it on the ELMO, that would make everybody's life easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, paragraph 2 in the B/C/S version, and page 2, paragraph 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph you say -- in the second paragraph you can read that you said, [In English] "Once a tape was full we would also give this to the commander. Then he would send the tape to the 2nd Corps headquarters and we would receive blank, secondhand tapes from 2nd Corps. However, if we did not have any blank tapes we would immediately record over tapes that we had at the side." [Interpretation] Do you remember that sometimes you re-use immediately on your site tapes which have already been used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? What do you mean, "immediately"?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Without sending them to the 2nd Corps command, you re-used them once they were full on the site where you were without sending them first to the command of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would happen on occasion, but never with the same tape which had previously been used by -- or with any of the devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you re-use --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you re-use the tapes you had already used and over which some conversations or intercepts were already taped? Did you re-use them to tape new conversations or intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When those -- that happened, however rare it was, in that case did you first erase the tape or would you directly tape again on the former conversation which was taped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the signature of the person who would type on the computer or the signature in the notebooks above the conversations. This is page 353 -- 953, do you remember how many persons in the team you were working with were in charge of typing those conversations on the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why in that case was it necessary for that person to sign the conversation in the notebook to be identified? Was it perfectly clear who was actually typing on the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each shift had its own typist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much I have no other question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who goes next? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My learned friend has asked me to confirm that I've got no cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Nor I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek is defending Mr. Beara and he will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I get a podium?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in November of 1999, you told them, and you've affirmed already that everything you've told them then was true, that you started your training after you arrived at the north location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you briefly tell me, describe for me the nature and length of that training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted for about a month, and I was shown all the equipment and I worked with it. I trained on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you recording conversations and then transcribing those conversations during that 30-day period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did any part of this training involve the use -- or involve voice recognition of participants that you might be intercepting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In fact, as I understand it, you, in 1999, could not remember any specific persons by recognising them by their voice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During this 30-day on-site training that you described, were you briefed by any persons with your army as to any members of the VRS that you might pay special or close attention to during your time there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only the locations and frequencies were mentioned. The ones we were supposed to monitor, not the people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit about the techniques you utilised when you listened to the tape recording. It's my understanding first that if you were listening to conversations that you might well listen to more than one; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if you were listening to more than one conversation can you give me an idea of the -- what was the most conversations that you might listen to at one given time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any given time, only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I think you indicated in your statement that some of the equipment you had could pick up -- the frequencies could pick up, up to 20 conversations; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot pick up 20 conversations, but rather each frequency was split into 24 parts, which were then scanned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So if the scanner is scanning 24 parts or -- and two -- say three conversations start at the same time, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment the most we could pick up were two conversations. The rest would go unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you be wearing headphones when you're listening to these conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if I'm correct, you would hear a conversation that you thought was interesting or important, and then you would push a button and start taping that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we would start recording, then we would see if it was interesting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then you recorded every conversation that you came upon until you decided it wasn't interesting and you stopped recording it, or decided that it was interesting and kept recording it. Is that what happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So, for example, if you came across the conversation, you started recording it, did you immediately start -- and you felt that it was interesting, did you immediately then start to write down what the participants were saying at that time, or did you just let it record and listen to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we would let the whole conversation be recorded, then we would listen back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you personally, was it your practice to take notes while you were just listening to the conversation in the first event while it was being recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Earlier this morning you've testified and answered questions that Ms. Fauveau put to you, in regards to the used tapes that you occasionally would have to use. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And at times you had new tapes, and at other times you had tapes that had been previously used and wiped clean and -- for re-use. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that the quality of the recording was much greater on a new tape than one that had been re-used more than one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on the 13th day of July can you tell me what time you started your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, can you remember, were you -- what time you would normally start your shifts when you had a day shift in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 12 years ago; I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You have no independent recollection, Witness, whatsoever? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember some things, but not when I did my shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe you testified yesterday that in regards to 65 ter Exhibit 1130A, B, C and D, the conversation that Mr. Vanderpuye, my learned colleague from the Prosecution asked you extensively about, that you discovered that was the 13th or you knew that was the 13th of July due to the night man having written down that date. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wondered if Mr. Meek would be so kind as to refer me to the page and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I would wonder if Mr. Vanderpuye would be so kind to show -- give the witness the notebook number 92 so we can look at it on the ELMO. Mr. Vanderpuye, I'm looking at 0800.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you say 0800, Mr. Meek? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, you are now looking at ERN number 00800801, which is contained in 65 ter 2322, which is notebook 92. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting at the top of page 0800 where it starts out "relativno" and then "dobro."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So if we back up two pages to 0798, that starts out 785.0 CH 20:07, is that your handwriting also, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What date was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was -- just one moment, please. It was probably the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, flipping back to 0800, is that your handwriting at the top of the page again, and then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What's that hand -- maybe we ought to go into closed session for just one moment, Judge, or private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Below the line that's drawn across the page, three quarters down, there is a 750.00, 3 channel, 00:10; below that, is that your handwriting, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So I believe from your testimony and your statement, that you gave to the OTP in 1999, you indicated that you would be working for approximately two hours, you would have six-hour shifts, you would work for about two hours listening and then another four hours recording, or transcribing what you heard. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the last that we see, if you go back to 0798, would have been on the 12th of July, 1995. You transcribed an intercepted conversation that was approximately two and three-quarter pages long; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I want to make sure I'm clear about this. At 10.07 p.m. on the 12th, you pushed a button and recorded a conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And does that help you refresh your recollection as to what time you quit your shift that night, the approximately two hours where you would tape record conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. It's -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, he -- in the transcript, and I actually heard you said 10.07, but what I see here is 20.07.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Military time always throws me off. It would be 8.00. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be fair, sir, looking at page 0798 of this document, that we know at least at 8.00, seven after 8.00 you had pushed a button and tape-recorded a conversation in an intercept. Fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in looking through that notebook, that was the last conversation that you taped that night before you quit, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that seemed to be a fairly lengthy conversation, at least in regards to the next conversation that someone else took at 10 minutes after midnight, which only lasted about five lines. And it's on 0800. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question. I don't think that it's at least a fair question in terms of counting the number of lines because you can see obvious differences in the size of the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer the question. He is not an uneducated, stupid man. He can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The conversation that you tape-recorded that started at seven minutes after 8.00 p.m. on the 12th was a fairly long conversation, at least in regards to some of the other ones that you took and other of your colleagues took, specifically the one directly below it that started at one [sic] after midnight on the 13th of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you normally took about four hours to listen to the tapes and write down and transcribe what you thought you heard from them, and you've already testified to that. So would it be a fair statement that you probably didn't finish transcribing the intercept that ended on 0800 until sometime after midnight on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well -- and this would not have been the only intercept that you transcribed after you went off your shift on the 12th, necessarily, would it be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it would be the only one you transcribed or it would be one of several or many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been one of several.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And according to your statement and testimony you always finished doing that transcription before you finalised your shift, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you might wait until the next day to listen to that tape and transcribe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that never happened. It had to be finished right after the shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You have notebook 92 in front of you. Why don't you just go back and tell the Court how many conversations you transcribed on your shift on the 12th and there -- or listened to on the 12th and thereafter transcribed after 8.07 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. According to this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What do you mean? You took this last one that started at 0798, we just talked about it. At 8.07 p.m., and you have -- I believe you testified that after you stopped your two-hour shift or so, you would then go and listen to this tape and write out what you thought you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I noted this text down during this shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that at times, once you had stopped the tape recording, for example, on this conversation, if there were no other conversations you needed to tape, you would immediately start listening to it, correct, and then transcribing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, do you have any independent recollection of what you did the evening of the 12th and when you finished transcribing that intercept that ended at 0800?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you also ask him whether he kept a copy of the menu for the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if you were using a new tape or a tape that had been taped over when you listened to the conversation that began on 0808 in your notebook, which you wrote down started at 10.09 a.m. on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It was put to you yesterday, and I'll have to ask you, was it very often -- let me rephrase that. How often, Witness, would it be that you would transcribe two full pages and then cross them out and start all over again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I made a mistake or when I didn't hear it properly and I wanted to hear it again, that piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would that happen once a week, once a month? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll put it to you, it didn't happen very often, did it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. We don't have the time here, but this notebook 92, and your handwriting is very distinctive. Do you agree with me that there is no where else in that whole notebook that you crossed out the way you did on this intercept, crossed out two full pages and then started again. Would you agree that's the only time you did it in that whole notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to look through the notebook in order to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll give you time to do that, Witness. Now, according to your testimony sometime after 10.09 a.m. in the morning of the 13th of July you began to transcribe the intercept in -- which you received, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you put down the participants of that, and again I'm going to refer you -- have you look at 0808. You are at 0800 at the top, those numbers. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Frequency 254.300, that was the frequency, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that was direction south, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you need to repeat your answer, because the interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that's what it was. I didn't note down the direction, only the frequency and the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you -- and I would ask the -- that 65 ter 11D, I believe it is, the transcribed version of this written intercept, be put on the ELMO. I'll just be one ... Here it is. Should be 1130 -- 65 ter number 1130B, I believe. On the e-court, I'm sorry. That's not it. I want the typed version. Yeah, okay. Do you see that? Witness, you speak English, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document as the typed version of your handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in English, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not in English, okay. But you see where it says 254.300?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That coincides with your handwritten notes on page 0808, which you have just been looking at to the right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. It says direction south, so that conversation was coming from the south. Is that what that means, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that in the handwritten text that's mine, this is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I understand it's not mentioned in the handwritten section, but that would be -- that frequency, to your knowledge, that's direction south, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I say that's what it's supposed to be, what it should be but I never noted down the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The direction was always noted down by whoever typed your handwritten notes; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And to your knowledge isn't Crna Rijeka, or the Black River, south of the location that you were at on that day on the 13th intercepting these conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, again looking back at your very first transcription, which is on 0808, I don't know if that's still on the ELMO for him or not, that he can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to go -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You have the participants down as Zokic -- Zoka, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Lucic, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And under Lucic you have "inaudible," don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You couldn't hear him at all, could you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What do you mean "probably," Witness? What do you mean probably? If you wrote down "inaudible," why do you tell us now probably you couldn't hear him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably because I wrote it down, it means that he couldn't be heard completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just -- I want again to have you look at what you crossed out, and you have a -- three dots which means inaudible, right, and then you have P-u-k Beara. Tell the court what P-u-k means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an abbreviation for colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you jump over to page 0810, could you move it a little bit? There you go. You have at this point decided you can't hear the tape well enough, you're going to cross out two pages and start all over. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you wrote down everything that you heard on the tape because you wanted to be as accurate as possible for your command, and that was part of the rules, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why is it that -- apparently you couldn't hear Colonel Beara when you started to re-listen to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be a fair statement that the quality of this tape was very, very poor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you this question: Do you have some problems with your hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's an objectionable question. I would ask the Court to countenance my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, let me just respond to that. It's not because he said -- he can't say whether the tape was bad, so the next question is, if the tape was fine, whether his hearing was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't think that's a reasonable inference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ask him to explain why he's saying so and not whether his hearing -- I mean, he hasn't shown any hearing impairment or deficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What other explanations -- if your hearing is perfect, your hearing is fine, and the tape is of good quality, what other explanations would it be that you couldn't hear that -- Colonel Beara when you started re-listening to the tape the second time when you heard it the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually one can hear one collocutor far better than the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you answer my question? Why is it, besides if the quality of the tape was fine and your hearing is fine, what other reason would it be that you did not hear Colonel Beara when you re-listened to the tape the second time when you, in fact, had already written it down when you first started listening to the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could it have been an equipment failure, that the equipment you were listening to it on just wasn't good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The equipment was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And as you just said, that -- the fact would be that most of these things you could always hear one of the participants better than another, or other participants, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, let's go back for a minute, because you've put "inaudible" on Lucic, but when we get to the typed-out version that the OTP did, which is an addition to tab 6, and I believe that would be 1130 -- I think E. Could that be shown to him on the screen in the e-court? Yeah. And I don't believe there is a B/C/S version of that. Okay. Leave that one on for a minute. Now, this is again -- what's on the screen now is an English translation of what you had crossed out in your two pages of handwritten notes. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then I will again just refer you back to 0808, the page that you first started crossing out this conversation. You have B, "Beara speaking." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again what does z-d-r-a-v-o "zdravo" in that 0808, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Greeting such as what? Hello? Is that, "Hello, Sjor Lucic, kako se"? I don't know if that's on the screen, sir, but in the handwritten notebook you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a standard greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I agree with you now, I want you to -- again, I don't know what you're looking at, do you have 0808 on the screen in front of you or just on the right? Is it on the screen too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What you think you are hearing is a person saying, "Colonel Beara," and then, "Hello, Sjor Lucic, how are you?" Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, where is the word "speaking" in there? Beara speaking, is the word "speaking" in B/C/S in there anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a word, but it's not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. After allegedly the person claiming to be Beara on this transcript or on this tape recording says, "How are you," look at your handwritten notes. What's the next word? You have "..." and then you have what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent or very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which is -- which means very well, correct? So is it my understanding that since Lucic was inaudible, that the person purported to be Beara asked Lucic how are you and then answered his own self that he was doing excellent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The dots should represent the other collocutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which would have been who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Nowhere in the transcribed English version is "odlicno" or "excellent" anywhere in there. Can you tell me why that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are, I think, two things that are going on. One is, I do see the word "excellent" actually in this transcript -- or this translation. The second thing is, I don't know if the witness has a basis of knowledge to speak to the veracity or accuracy of the English translation. And I think that in that regard the questions are irrelevant as put to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, the translations that we have are translations made for us, that's number one. They are not translations originating from the same offices or facilities or commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Judge. I'll skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll just ask the witness then to go back and flip, if you would, to the notebook page where you decided you couldn't hear and you were going to start over, and you did that at 0810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could ask the witness if he sees in the translation the word "excellent," which admittedly there is. What is purported to be the translation of the crossed-out part. Okay? You can ask him whether that indeed shows up, whether there is the equivalent word in B/C/S in the handwritten --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's just what I was going to ask him, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Please turn to page 0810 in your diary, Witness. The notebook. Do you have it? In the notebook to your right on the ELMO. Where you started re-transcribing it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, you're going to agree with me that there is no word "odlicno" or "excellent" in that second one, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard you say odlicno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, on page 0808, I do see "odlicno" on the third line of the script, which is cancelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I asked the witness to go to 0810 where he decides to start -- re-begin his transcription of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's not there, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In fact, we can go on and on about the things that aren't there from the first to the second, can't we, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you believe, sir, that your listening to this tape-recorded conversation the second time you could hear it any better than you could the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably why I cancelled the first one and started anew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. But apparently that's why you did, but then you started the new one and right away you don't pick up Colonel Beara, and two sentences later you don't pick up "excellent," correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And maybe I've already asked you this and if I did I'm sure you're going to tell me. You don't know if that was a new tape or a used tape that had been taped over and over again, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on the second one, and again I refer you to 0810, where you restarted it, and yesterday the learned Judge A. Agius asked you why it was you didn't put the participants, the frequency number and the time, and you answered because it was a continuation of the same conversation, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and maybe you can't answer this, but maybe you can. When we finally get a transcription or when it goes to -- we get an English transcription, we have the participants being Beara, Lucic, and it says, "Lucic and Zoka (barely audible)" instead of "(inaudible)"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then I would ask that 65 ter 1130C be put on the e-court for this witness for just a moment. All right. And for the record, this is the end result of the typist, encryptionist typing out your handwritten notes, correct? Now, do you see in B/C/S in your own language, the participants? Right under direction south, direction J? See it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It says, "Beara -- and Lucic Zoka (barely audible)" isn't that what it says? Isn't that what it says, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if you can tell me this, who was barely audible, Zoka? Or Lucic and Zoka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about my text or the typed-out version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about yours, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that. He's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then as far as -- in your version, it's completely inaudible, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And now in the typed version all of a sudden it becomes barely audible and we don't even know who it is that's barely audible or Zoka or Lucic and Zoka both; fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask the person who did the encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would like to do that sometime. Then you wrote down the time. You wrote down this conversation was taped at 10.09 a.m., didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then on 65 ter 1130C, which is in front of you on the screen, that conversation came in at 10.15 a.m. on the 13th, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You didn't recognise this person that you put down as Beara, you didn't recognise his voice, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You did recognise his voice or you did not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony you told the Prosecutor when he asked you the question --.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That would be on page 66 of yesterday's transcripts, Your Honours, line starting at 17 through 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor even asked you some questions about the typed version and you answered on line 17 "I don't know in the typewritten text." Which you just answered to me about some questions, and I understand that. The Prosecutor then asked you, "Okay. Now, with respect to what you have written in your notebook versus any other document that you may have reviewed, which would you consider the more authoritative or accurate?" Your answer, "Mine, of course." Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's pretty clear, and I would like to take you back to the original notebook, 0812. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We have been told by the Prosecutor before you testified that you actually looked and reviewed the notebook and the printout of this intercept. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you say in particular the phrase on that page, 0812, "Daj mi ga," or, "Let me talk to him," or "Put him on," is attributed to B, Beara in the printout, and to Lucic in the notebook. In any event, Witness, look at page 0812. When the person speaking says, "Put him on" or "Let me talk to him," "Daj mi ga," that's in your handwritten, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you have that as being Lucic saying that, don't you, even though the typed version had Beara saying that? You in your own handwriting had Lucic saying that, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that's more authoritative than the typed -- or the typed version, isn't it, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So I'll come back to that in just a moment. Did you know at the time or do you know now, and have you learned since that time or did you know at the time, that Zoka was the nickname for Zoran Malinic and that Lucic and Zoran Malinic were both stationed at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that the more authoritative of the typed version and your handwritten notes, are your handwritten notes and it was Lucic who said let me talk to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my version, yes, Lucic said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then thereafter every time that you have a B for Beara, it should have been an L for Lucic because that's the voice you heard saying, "Let me speak to him." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it seems like to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I'll just wrap this up. I'm sure you worked hard, you didn't have much sleep, and this was a poor recording, and you couldn't tell one voice from the other. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case I could probably hear Beara very well, whereas Lucic I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then when we get down to the page where Lucic wants to speak with Zoka, that's the same voice you thought was Beara's. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this is unfair on the witness and you are confusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He already answered that question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because he told you his terms by what there is in the -- in the transcript. He agreed ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I would just refer the Court to the question that I started at page 31, line 20, and this witness's response at line 23 on page 31, and with that, Your Honour, I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but just to be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I clarify one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you take a look at the page 0809 of the notebook? This is part of the crossed-out transcription where you said that you cannot hear Lucic very well, or inaudible, et al, right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the bottom part you can see, "Aha, daj mi ga." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One can see that that is the voice of Beara according to what you said so far. Am I correct in so assuming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. That's why it was crossed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Thank you. Let me be clear. So what you just said is that's the reason why you crossed that part, two pages? Is that what you said right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I crossed out these two pages was that I could hear another voice in the background, and I wanted to listen to it again and try and make out what it was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the voice who said "daj mi ga" was another voice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question to -- to you in addition to what my colleague, Judge Kwon has asked you is the follows: Forget the typewritten versions of what is alleged to be your entry, forget them for the time being. Forget the handwritten entry in the notebook which you crossed out. Forget that. Concentrate on the next handwritten entry, which is the second -- your second attempt to transcribe that intercept. In that entry you put, against the various intercepted words, letters: B, L, and later on Z. Having testified here now for all this time, and having been asked questions by not only counsel for the Prosecution, but also Defence counsel, is there any entry there attributed to any of the individuals that those three letters, B, L and Z represent that you would concede is wrongly attributed to that person in your entry? In other words, for example, Judge Kwon asked you as regards the words, "Aha, daj mi ga." If you look at 0812, that appears to have been said according to you, by Lucic or Lukic. Lucic. Do you stand by that or could that be mistakenly attributed to Lucic and should have been attributed to someone else? Is there any such words or expressions in your entry in the notebook for that intercepted conversation that you would like to draw our attention to as being mistakenly attributed to a particular person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text there were two lines, rather we have Beara and Lucic. "Aha, daj mi ga," most certainly is not something that should be attributed to Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I take it from what I had heard that there are no other cross-examinations. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is a brief re-examination, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to this particular area of conversation, and that is the phrase, "daj mi ga," that you have attributed to Mr. Lucic in your handwritten transcription of this intercept, you've indicated to the Court that you are -- you stand by your attribution of that phrase to Mr. Lucic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or to someone on his end or at his end of the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what follows this phrase, "Daj mi ga," that is the continued conversation between -- as you have indicated in your handwritten material, a continued conversation between Zoka and Beara, do you stand what is contained in your handwritten transcription?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having reviewed this material and given it some thought during examination by Defence counsel and also by the Court, can you provide any explanation for why you have made this particular attribution in light of what follows in your written transmission -- written transcription?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please reformulate?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can do that. I think the gist of what's being asked of you is, if you have attributed the phrase "daj mi ga" to Mr. Lucic, then reasonably what should follow is a conversation between Zoka and Mr. Lucic? What you have in your written transcript is a conversation that follows between Zoka and Mr. Beara. Now, having had that put to you, and having given it some thought, can you, if you can, do you have an explanation for why that is the case or as it appears in your -- in what you wrote down in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-124 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The voice came from Lucic's side. You can see from the conversation that Zoka and Lucic were on the same line, so either one of them could have said that. It could have been in the background that Zoka said "daj mi ga," but anyway it was at that end of the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I'm going to object to the speculative nature of this answer, and I -- further, I don't even believe this is proper redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is proper re-examination, obviously, because it arises out of what you asked and also what I asked. The -- and there is no speculative element to the question either. In fact, I'm going to rephrase your question myself because I think it is very important. And it will hopefully shed enough lighten enabling us to decide what weight, if at all, to give to this -- this transcript in particular. It's been put to you, as follows, Witness. And could you please go to 0812 from the notebook? So I take you back again to those words attributed to Lucic according to you, and you have confirmed that. "Aha, daj mi ga," which translated into English is "Ah-ha let me talk to him." And then you have Zoka or Z who says "Da." Mr. Vanderpuye is suggesting to you that if "aha, daj mi ga," are words that were spoken by Lucic to Zoka, and if Zoka replied, as is obvious from the transcript itself, then the rest of the conversation should have been between Lucic and Zoka and not between Beara and Zoka. If you look at the notebook, what you have after the "da" then it's Beara's, "Zdravo, Zoka." And then Zoka who is inaudible, and Beara "Sta, ima novo," and then Zoka and then Beara and then Zoka and then Beara, and then Zoka. It is being suggested to you that if the words, "Aha, daj mi ga" by Lucic in other words it was Lucic looking for Zoka, the rest of the conversation would be between those two and not between Beara and Zoka. Do you have any explanation for this? I don't any if I have misrepresented your question, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I think it's a pretty fair assessment of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two sides in each conversation. One -- you can hear one better, the other one not so well. In this case, one collocutor, Beara in this case, could be heard very well. So I had no doubts that it was him. The other end where Lucic was, and this text, "Aha, daj mi ga," Zoka could said that in the background, but he was at the other end of the line, the other end that could not be heard as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a couple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that it is entirely possible that -- well, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to conclude as quickly as you can, because we should have had the break about eight minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and conclude, please. Unless I have objections from -- if anyone insists that we have the break now, I will have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think we ought to have the break, judge, because I'm going to have some re-examination when he gets done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, for the record, Mr. McCloskey is not present now. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I just only have maybe a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, you had indicated in response to the Court's question that the phrase "daj mi ga" as you have attributed it to Mr. Lucic may have been the result of some confusion, may perhaps -- should have been attributed to somebody else, maybe Zoka or somebody on that end of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. That is not exactly what he said. You are saying should have been. He never said it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's saying it may have been or could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That it may be the case that it should -- that would more properly have been attributed to someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he never conceded that. He said that came -- those words were uttered from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Lucic end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. But there was more than one person speaking at that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If that were the case, that it was someone other than Lucic who had uttered those words, but from the Lucic end of the conversation, then what follows that transition, would that make sense in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't there is a need for that question. Let us draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In that case I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So, do you have questions, Judge Kwon? There are no further questions for you, sir. What is the matter, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Nothing is the matter, Your Honour. I would just like to say I have no further re-cross-examination other than the fact that should, in the future, at some point Your Honours want to admit this notebook 92 in its entirety, I would like the Court to take judicial notice that this witness, this was the only intercept where he crossed out two pages and there are no other intercepts where he crossed out even slightly close to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I thank you, Mr. Meek, for that observation. I was tempted at the time to -- to concede that to you, because obviously you're right, there doesn't seem to be any other pages. All right. Sir, that brings your testimony to an end. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come to give testimony. Our staff will assist you making -- concluded the arrangements necessary for your return. On behalf of everyone, we wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, documents, exhibits. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We propose to tender at this time the witness statement PO2345 and the pseudonym sheet under seal PO2346 in evidence, and then offer for -- to be marked for identification, subject to connection later on -- okay. I think everybody has a copy of the tender sheet. And I would just -- I don't want to necessarily go through all of them, but everything on it I would offer for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. With the understanding that those documents that appear in bold --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Should be tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again those will be marked for identification purposes only for the time being pending final determination of the issues relating to intercepts and to the notebook. Yes, now there is also under 1379D an audio tape, which we didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ah. With respect to the audio tape, I would -- well, we'll have it marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't made use of it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's true. I don't believe we're ultimately going to submit it, but if it's only marked for identification purposes, perhaps that's okay at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Agreed. Any objections on the part of the Defence teams, apart from the usual caveats in relation to this category or this class of documents? I hear none. So they are so admitted as stated earlier. Any of the Defence team wishes to tender any documents? I see none. So that brings the Witness PW-124 chapter to an end. Let me clear up what I have in front of me first. So now there are some housekeeping matters that we have to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a question to Mr. Meek. Notebook 92 hasn't been tendered. Would it be okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's try to do this exercise in a logical way. I think we need to start first with the Popovic Defence motion pursuant to Rule 127 A for the extension of time to file a response to the Prosecution's submission of the 9th of January, 2007. This Popovic Defence motion was filed on the 11th of January. We are handing now an oral decision. If required by you, Mr. Zivanovic, we'll follow up with a written decision. If not, the oral decision will stand, will suffice. Our decision is to reject your request for 14-days time since the filing of the OTP submission to respond and challenge the OTP submissions that you referred to in your motion. The reasons are as follows: We are of the opinion that a copy of the intercept and the intercept book was -- has been available for a sufficient time to enable you to take stock of or familiarise yourself with its contents. The second, there is no legal justification for your submission that you haven't had time to go through the OTP submissions, and, in fact, this in itself is contradicted by the rest of the motion which deals precisely with the submissions. The rest you can deal with in your cross-examination. However, having disposed of your motion as is, I now call upon you, and I will be calling upon the others as well, your other colleagues, to make any oral submissions now on the Prosecution 9th January submission. And we will start with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to have your written decision on this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. As I said, once you have asked for a written decision, you will also have a written decision, will be along the lines that you have just explained in our oral decision. But that's the decision already, in other words, you are now asked to proceed with your oral submissions in response to the Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I would like to say is the following: In the submission given to us by the Prosecutor two days before bringing the witness into the courtroom is in my assessment lacking in stating valid reasons why this evidence was not proposed for use earlier. The Prosecutor analysed evidence or analysed the intercept itself. I believe that the whole point of the Prosecutor was to, by having a positive decision from you, to have the intercept placed on the list, and also to accept the reasons and the analysis of the intercept itself, with which we do not happen to agree. What we wanted to have an opportunity to state our position on is also to be given enough time to do that, even though it's not as much time as the Prosecutor had, and we would like to dispute the validity of the analysis provided by the Prosecutor on this analysis. Especially we would like to deal with the reasons why the intercept was not placed on the list of exhibits right away, even though it had been available for the past four years. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would anyone, any other Defence team like to make oral submissions? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time I would like to support the objections made by my colleague, and the object of my submission is to respectfully request the Trial Chamber not to allow the Prosecution to add the proposed 20 April intercept to which Rule 65 ter list of exhibits and consequently to rule that the testimony of Witness 77 is no longer relevant and necessary. As a background to my submission, Mr. President, the Defence would like to recall that the 20 April intercept was not on the Prosecution's list on Rule 65 list of exhibits, nor was it mentioned in two Prosecution motions to modify its list of exhibits in both August and September. The first time that the 20 April intercept was mentioned is in the Prosecution motion of 21 November in which it requested Witness 77 to be changed from Rule 92 bis to Rule 92 ter in accordance with the Trial Chamber's ruling on 92 bis, the -- its 92 bis ruling. Now, the Defence immediately opposed this motion from the Prosecution and on the basis that the Prosecution had not exercised due diligence in bringing the intercept, nor provided any information as to the need to use this intercept in the first place. Now, nonetheless, we agreed at the time to change Witness 77 from Rule 92 bis to Rule 92 ter because there was at the time 22 intercepts in the whole package. Of course, Mr. President, as mentioned yesterday we now know that 20 of those intercepts are -- were not transcribed by Witness 77 and had we known this fact, we would have also objected to even changing the witness from 92 bis to 92 ter. The Prosecution replied to our response, that was a few days later, and for the first time they attempted to justify the use of the 20 April intercept. And what they said, they said three things: They said that the intercept goes to the acts and conduct of the accused; they said that it was during the period relevant to the indictment; and they said that it was critical to the Trial Chamber's understanding of the events without saying why. Now, even though we did not have an opportunity to respond to these three arguments, of course we were ready to say at the time that even though the name Nikolic may be on that intercept, there is nothing in the material which was provided by the Prosecution which says that the intercept actually corresponds to Nikolic, the accused in this case. The second thing is about the relevant period, it was said -- Prosecution said that it was the relevant period but now they recognise that the intercept, which dates of 20 April, 1995, is outside of the period relevant to the indictment. They actually used the date to say this is why they did not look at the intercept in the first place. Then the Prosecution says the events are not related to Srebrenica. On the 13 December the Trial Chamber gave its ruling and said, yes, Witness 77 can testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter, but if the Prosecution wants to use this 20 April intercept it would have to use -- they would have to show good cause. In other words, our understanding is that the Trial Chamber invited the Prosecution to make an application so that we could consider whether this 20 April intercept could be added to its list of -- this Rule 65 ter list. As we know, the Prosecution filed on 15 December, it filed an application to add 10 more intercepts on its list, but not this one. It didn't do anything. Despite the chamber's ruling of 13 December, it did not even try to get this intercept on its rule 65 ter list, and it's only on 9 January that they give us this new application, a few days ago, in which they argue three things, and I would like to argue three things to show that good cause has not been shown in the circumstances. First of all, the Prosecution says that the OTP initially focused on intercepts from the June to October 1995 period, and that is why they missed this particular intercept dated from April. First of all, it is on the record, and I hear -- I join the submissions of my colleague, that the Prosecution has been in possession of all intercept material at the latest on 13 December 2000. Now I say that is on the record because if we look back to the testimony of P 131, this is what we get. Now, the argument that they did not look at this particular intercept because it was outside of the relevant period doesn't stand when we look at the fact that there are intercepts outside of this period on its list. So why would it have missed this one but not the others? And then a third one is that of course this argument confirms that 20 April is indeed outside of the relevant period of this indictment. That was the first Prosecution submission. In the second one, the Prosecution concedes the intercept is not related to the Srebrenica events. So immediately its relevance goes very much down unless there is a very specific reason to use the intercept. In response what we say is that this intercept mentions first of all again I go back to the fact that we don't know whether this is Nikolic the accused in this case or not. Again, this goes to whether this is relevant. There is no indication that the witness can tell us whether this is really Nikolic or not. And then if we look at the content of the intercept, it deals with two Polish volunteers. Now, Mr. President, this is a case of an alleged genocide against Bosnian Muslims. Two Polish volunteers in that case simply has nothing to do with the fact that whether or not this intercept is relevant. It can have no probative value and no relevance to the issues in this case.
