The third argument raised by the Prosecution is that they say that the 20 April intercept is part of a small group of intercepts involving the accused Popovic and Nikolic. Indeed, Mr. President, they're right. There are no intercepts involving these two accused. There are a very limited number of intercepts where we even find the name Nikolic without even knowing if it is the Nikolic in this case. Now, the other intercept that is referred to by the Prosecution dates back to 19 January. Again, way outside of the relevant period of this indictment. Moreover, for that 19 January intercept, they don't have an operator and they don't have a notebook. And that would be contrary to the Trial Chamber's decision that if there is something that goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, there must be the operator who would testify this case. Finally, Mr. President, the Prosecution adds that if the Trial Chamber decides to use this 20 April intercept, then it will follow up with another request to add three more documents on the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. Three more documents they found after. Once they find the 20 April intercept, now they find three our documents in their collection that comes from the Drina Corps. Now we're back to square one, Mr. President, and the question is, when will this end? When this going around in circles end and when will the Defence be finally informed of what the Prosecution's case entails? The last part of this submission, Mr. President, we respectfully submit that the Prosecution has not shown good cause. Good cause is two things: Why the document was in the on the list in the first list, and there has been no due diligence in this case. They have had these intercepts for more than six years. They have had all the time in the world to find the intercept, they did not put the intercept on the list, and due diligence is simply lacking in this case. As to the alleged critical need for the use of this document, when we look at the relevance, what the document talks about, that it's not related to Srebrenica, that it's not related in terms of date and that we have no link that we know of that it is linked to one of the accused in this case. For this reason, good cause has not been shown. In conclusion, when we look at Witness 77, if we take away the 20 intercepts that are not his, that's what the Prosecution told us, then we're back -- we have two intercepts. One of those the Prosecution has recognised, and I am -- undoubtedly my colleague will say so, that it is not critical and that it does not go to the acts and conduct of the accused. So in the end we're back with only one intercept and that is the intercept of 20 April, which was not originally on the Prosecution's list. So in conclusion, Mr. President, unless the Trial Chamber has a burning desire to hear another witness that we will put questions to as to how difficult it was to transcribe intercepts, I simply suggest respectfully that Witness 77 will not -- should not testify today and should be sent home, and that would be the end of the matter. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to add two things in view of your decision today. First, I believe that this analysis of the intercept, according to the Prosecutor indicates -- that the intercept of the 20th of April indicates ethnic intolerance on the part of my client. I'm only speaking on behalf of my client now, does not stand, and this is evident from the contents of the intercept, and that is why I believe that this should not be a reason to accept this intercept and have it on the Prosecutor list. It should not be the one valid reason that the Prosecutor is justifying for leaving out this intercept from the original 65 ter list. I also believe that the reason to accept this intercept should not be the one also given by the Prosecutor and that is that this intercept actually proves the veracity or the authenticity of all the other intercepts which come from different locations and different time periods, which were picked up and transcribed. Especially the evidence that he bases this conclusion on, and these exhibits are not on the list. And the Prosecutor said that. He is talking about the death of one of the two volunteers, without saying when and what the circumstances of the deaths were, and this happens five or six months before in a completely different location, in a completely different place. So I believe that those two reasons should not be the reasons based on which the intercept is being placed on the Prosecutor's 65 ter list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, the Defence for Mr. Beara also joins these objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further oral submissions? Would you like to respond if -- you haven't had time either to respond to Mr. Zivanovic's motion for delay in any case. So could you now respond to the submissions made by the three learned counsel, Zivanovic, Bourgon and Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President, and I will do my best to keep it brief. With respect to the good cause argument, Your Honours, I won't belabour our 9 January submission. I think we've explained that fully, and I don't think it would be helpful at this point to go into any more detail than we have already unless the Court has further inquiries about the explanation provided in the submission. I think it's quite clear; the chronology, which my learned colleague Mr. Bourgon correctly stated. This was something that was discovered after the Court's 12 September 92 bis decision as we were expands the search, and I will just leave it there with respect to the good cause argument for failing to list that on the 65 ter witness list. Let me just jump directly to the relevance of -- of the intercept, and respond to a couple of things that my learned colleague Mr. Bourgon stated. First of all, the Prosecution has never stated that the June to October date range is the relevant date range for the indictment. Obviously is belied by the document itself. The date range refers only to the common-sensical period for the thousands of intercepts we had in the collection. Given the military operation in Srebrenica and the aftermath, looking from June to October seemed like that was the most potentially fruitful area to do the intensive search that has led to the vast, vast majority of the intercepts which have been offered here and which we will continue to offer. So we are talking about two different time-frames, obviously, for those purposes. What I would point out is that we are arguing obviously that the intercept, when taken in context with the additional documents that we have referred to in the submission, and I'll pick up on my learned colleague's Mr. Zivanovic's final point, do go directly to the issue that has recently been raised by several Defence counsel as to the reliability and, in fact, the actual authenticity of these intercepts. The suggestion that, in fact, they have been fabricated or they were created sometime after the events which the notebooks purport to have recorded them. When we look at this intercept and the documents which the Prosecution has referred to, we see that they are right on point with each other, they are absolutely corroborative of one another. These are Main Staff and Drina Corps documents ultimately going down to the Zvornik Brigade which coincide absolutely perfectly with the content of this intercept. It also shows, as we noted in the submission, the relationship between the Popovic and Nikolic individuals in the conversation. It shows the flow of the chain of command, which are important for the Court to see, how that works in practice. Fortuitously, this intercept was made at the time, and we can see here an absolutely perfect example of the job that these intercept operators were doing. We would submit, Your Honours, that this is probative, relevant evidence that is ultimately helpful to the Court in its decision-making both in respect of the admissibility, reliability, and authenticity of these intercepts as well as the other issues I just raised, the relationships between these individuals, the operation of the chain of command, and again the bias which -- which we will argue is exhibited in the text of the conversation. Again, with respect to the analysis that was referred to by my learned colleague Mr. Zivanovic, that's for another day and I won't burden the Court with that now. I think, as we understand it, that will be a matter for later submissions. What we are asking the Trial Chamber to do, Your Honours, is to continue its case-by-case assessment of these requests to add to our 65 ter exhibit and witness list. We believe that the Trial Chamber has struck in its 6 December and 11, I believe, January rulings the appropriate balance between emphasising, prioritising the rights of the accused but at the same time admitting relevant probative evidence to come before this Court. We believe that during the four previous months the trial has not been burdened or slowed appreciably because of some of our prior requests. We are doing our best to limit the future requests, but I think we all recognise that these kinds of things will emerge. I believe the Prosecution believes that the Court's approach thus far is faithful to Rule 73 bis F, but also ultimately to the general discretion as proposed in the Trial Chamber in 89 C and D, and ultimately this is a matter of truth-seeking, and we would submit that this intercept and the related documents, when taken in context, ultimately further that search, and I will leave it there, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting for the third time. I will try to clarify what I said previously. Again, I wish to stress the following: The Prosecutor was ordered by the Bench to state their reasons as to why this intercept had not been put on the list previously, and they put forth some reasons, but everything else they said as to the importance and relevance of the transcript -- of the intercept is not the reason why they did not put it on the list. It should have been the reason why they should have put it. And it is no justification, no excuse for not putting it on the list. I'm trying to say the following: I have nothing against the Prosecutor writing whatever they want in their brief or submission. They can analyse whatever piece of evidence they wish, but what I want for my part to be given sufficient time to respond to that analysis. At the moment when they should show good reason for not putting an exhibit on the list, since they had it in their possession for five years and they give it to us two days before having the witness here, they topped that with an additional analysis which leaves us with less than one day to respond to. I don't believe that is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Briefly, firstly the Prosecution said that they would not go back on their 9 January filing. Of course they have not explained again why six year in possession of this material and they can't come up with a coherent case six years later. Secondly, most importantly, they said, "We will continue to offer intercepts." That means that they are still looking at these intercepts and that the case will keep changing. As the case keeps changing, then of course delays will pile up. Then they say of course this has to be looked with the additional documents of those documents are not on the record and those documents of course we will object to having those documents put on the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. What is accepted by the Defence at all times, Prosecution can continue to investigate, but this is not a continued investigation. This is going back to material in their possession for six years. That's what we mean when we talk about a -- the right of an accused to be charged -- to be tried within a reasonable delay. Six years with this material is just too much. 10 years working on Srebrenica is too much. Should they find a new witness that nobody knew about that's something out of the ordinary and that is both critical to the Trial Chamber's understanding, maybe then we can argue and maybe we can understand that there is a need to add something. But now we're talking about an intercept that has no relevance, that they had for six years, and there is no reason for that not to be there. Then they show on the contents they say they want to show the flow of the chain of command. Well, to begin with, they should show the flow of the chain of command in July. But they do not have any intercepts in July or June or August that involve Mr. Popovic and Mr. Nikolic. Over and above the fact of course we don't know if these are the right individuals, but leaving that aside they don't know, they have nothing about these two individuals speaking during the relevant period. So in order to patch up this -- what is missing in their case, they go back to one intercept of January, two people talking together, and one intercept of April that is unrelated. So, Mr. President, they are building up their case as they go along. They're trying to do patch-up work with evidence that was in their possession for a long time. And my colleague said, this has not slowed the proceedings. Well, if I just look at all the filings, all the arguments, everything that we have been receiving concerning this Witness 77 and this one intercept since the 21st of November, this has been indeed a significant cause of delay in this case, as it is again today. Now, I'm offering the Trial Chamber really an opportunity to really show some judicial restraint and do the right thing for the rights of the accused and say Prosecution that's enough. You've had the material, let's move on and get to the next witness, and that's what I'm offering the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a short break so that we can deliberate further and conclude and we will come back to you with an oral decision in a few minutes' time. --- Break taken at 11.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, this is an oral decision that we are giving pursuant to the Prosecution's 9th January, 2007 submission, which in turn is pursuant to our 12th September, 2006 decision on Prosecution's confidential motion for admission of written evidence in lieu of viva voce testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Having previously disposed of Popovic Defence motion pursuant to Rule 127 A for the extension of time to file a response of the Prosecution's submission by rejecting same, having heard submissions by -- oral submissions from the parties we provide as follows: The first matter in issue was to decide whether the Prosecution has, in conformity with our 13th December decision, identified the specific written evidence of Witness 77, which it proposes for admission pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In addition to the fact that we have not heard objections in relation -- we have in the received objections in relation to this issue, we are satisfied that, as explained in paragraph 3 of the Prosecution's submission, that this requirement has been met and therefore that there are no further obstacles to having Witness 77 testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. That disposes of the first matter. Second matter relates to intercept 1 in Annex A, which is better described in the filings and decisions that preceded this one. The matter at issue indeed is whether to include the said intercept, or the intercept in question, and the Prosecution's 65 ter list. As per our 13th December decision, before the Prosecution could have this intercept included in their 65 ter list, it was required from them to show good cause. The Trial Chamber believes that the threshold required in the exercise -- for the purpose of this exercise is not a high one and can be met on a prima facie basis. We have considered the contents of the Prosecution 9th January submissions and also the arguments put forward by three of the Defence teams today, and we are satisfied that -- basing ourselves on what is contained in paragraph 5 of the Prosecution 9th January filing, we are satisfied that the threshold has been sufficiently met and we are consequently persuaded that a good cause has been shown. The Trial Chamber is also persuaded that at prima facie level, the alleged relationship between the two mentioned accused, that is Popovic and Nikolic, is of relevance to the case again on a prima facie level. This ruling of course is without prejudice to the arguments and submissions pertinent to the ultimate determination of admissibility and weight issues. Our decision therefore in relation to this intercept is to accede to the Prosecution request in having it included in the Prosecution's 65 ter motion. As with the case of the Popovic Defence motion, we will follow up with a proper written version of this decision in due course. So, that disposes of the matters relating to Witness number 77, but not completely. And Witness 77 we are pooling with all the remaining intercept operator witnesses and as we intimated yesterday, after having given this matter further thought, we are going to hand down an order. We expressed to you yesterday that after having heard the evidence of several intercept operator witnesses, including the one whose evidence -- whose testimony we have concluded a few minutes ago, we have had growing concerns about the way we have been proceeding. We have intimated to you that the way examination-in-chief and cross-examination have been carried out has resulted, in our opinion, in unduly lengthy evidence, which, in many instances has, indeed, been repetitive and in some instances - we maintain this position - has been of marginal relevance at best. We consider that much of the evidence that has been elicited from the various witnesses amounts to unnecessary cumulative evidence, and is therefore of minimal -- and is also of minimal relevance. We reiterate our responsibility that we have in our duty to ensure the fair and expeditious conduct of this trial, and the order that we will be handing down aims at addressing both the question of fairness and also the question of expediting the proceedings in a reasonable manner. In view of this, and after carefully considering the various submissions that you made yesterday, we have come to the following conclusion, which we are incorporating by way of a court order. As from now the Prosecution shall be permitted a maximum of 30 minutes for examination-in-chief of each intercept operator witness. The Defence collectively shall be permitted a maximum of two hours and 20 minutes for cross-examination of each witness. The way we intend this to proceed is as follows: At the earliest opportunity, but not longer soon after the end of the examination-in-chief the Defence teams shall inform the Trial Chamber if agreement has been reached between them as to the sharing, the partition of the said time limit allowed for cross-examination. If no such agreement has been reached, each Defence team will have at its disposal a maximum of 20 minutes for cross-examining each witness. However, upon good cause being shown, parties will be permitted by the Trial Chamber to exceed these limits. There is also one further matter that we need to bring to your attention, and that these limitations will not be applicable in the case of any MUP intercept operator witnesses. While the Chamber, having heard your various submissions yesterday, will not restrict any party from asking relevant, probative questions, we would make the following recommendations to you: We feel that considerable evidence regarding the general interception of communications and the applicable procedures, as well as equipment used, has already been heard. Therefore, in the case of the Prosecution we would recommend that the evidence summaries be reduced to cover only and merely the specifics of each particular witness, as the case may be. Similarly, we would suggest that counsel for accused should focus their future questioning of individual intercept operators on the specific communications intercepted personally by the witness being examined. The examination should avoid, as much as possible, repetitive evidence on the procedures, equipment and other matters related to the interception process generally, which have been covered already at length by several previous witnesses, unless of course a good reason is forthcoming for putting such a question, in which case we will allow such questions. This is our decision. I know that very soon we shall have Witness number 77 walk in the courtroom to start giving evidence. I don't know if you wish to have five minutes to discuss amongst yourselves how you wish to partition the time allocated. We won't have another break after now. In other words, we will then adjourn at quarter to 2.00. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We take good note of the Trial Chamber's decision and at this time I would respectfully request the permission to do an oral application for certification of the Trial Chamber's decision concerning the fact that the Trial Chamber's decision that good cause has been shown by the Prosecution. I can either make that -- this application orally or make it in writing but we would need -- we would respectfully submit that the witness could not testify until this matter has been resolved both for certification and in the event certification is granted that the appeal has been resolved. We feel this is a very important issue for the conduct of this case. If the Prosecution is allowed to show good cause on such limited material with six years with that material in their possessions, that means for us that everything open, that they can put any document that they have, that they can find any new documents that so in the simple reason that we have the Drina Corps collection, which includes a million pages untranslated, that now they can use anything at any time in this case and, for us, it is an issue that we indeed need that we have to appeal. And that is why I can either make this application orally or writing. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do you wish to response respond to that, Mr. McCloskey, or Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would leave that entirely in the Court's hands. We are prepared to argue against certification now. The witness is here. I don't see any impediment, frankly, to getting on with his testimony and getting on with any appellate issues later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. There is no point in hearing submissions on the certification oral request that has been made if we have already intimated that the written version of our decision will be -- will be handed down. I need of course -- it is not a decision that I can take, and I would never even think of taking. I need to consult my colleagues on the issue on whether to await the decision on the certification before we proceed with the testimony of this witness. Certainly other submissions I don't -- I don't think they are appropriate at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, it's needless or superfluous to say that we have been discussing, and our decision at the moment is as follows: Mr. Bourgon is the only one who stood up to register his objection or his reservations on our decision, on our decision relating to the intercept, that's what we're talking about. First of all, we would like it know whether there are any other Defence teams that also wish to make submissions, oral submissions by way of substantiating an oral request for certification. Yeah, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, the Defence for Mr. Beara certainly joins in the motion by Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will probably also join the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now at this point I think I'm almost -- yes, I apologise to the interpreters. I moved too fast. At this point I think we need -- Mr. Bourgon, we need to go a little bit beyond what we have done so far. The Prosecution has said okay, certification matters, we'll leave them in your hands. But we need to hear more in-depth submissions on the part of the Defence in particular, Mr. Bourgon, by way of substantiating your, or explaining why the Trial Chamber should grant certification. I think what you have stated is good, but it is very laconic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do I understand that the Trial Chamber's ruling is that you want an oral application at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have already, as far as we are concerned, we have an oral application for certification. Let's take it step by step. We handed down our oral decision. Okay? You have intimated that you are not happy with it, and that you were asking orally for a certification, and that in the meantime, pending the final determination of the matter that we decided earlier on, either by us not granting certification or if we grant certification by the final decision from the Appeals Chamber, in the meantime Witness number 77 will not be heard. This is basically the position, as I understand it. This is what you have submitted. Right. So there are various issues to be discussed. First and foremost is why, according to you, in addition to what you have already stated, we should grant certification. We don't want to listen why -- why our decision is wrong. Please limit yourself to the grounds that are provided by our regulations which form or should form the basis for a Trial Chamber decision to grant certification. Okay, yes, Rule 73 B. I mean, you know as much as I do that the Rules, our law, does not give an automatic right of appeal. It's limited, and it's limited, there are parameters that have to be met and within which we have to operate. So what I am inviting you to do, and of course others can -- can follow you, is to address these issues. Not trying to explain why in your opinion our decision is wrong. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I must say that I really, really appreciate the Trial Chamber's invitation to make this oral application without referring to the decision itself because indeed whether the Trial Chamber believes its decision is right or whether I believe it's wrong is irrelevant in -- in the matter of asking for certification. So whether it's wrong, right or wrong is not the issue. The issue is the consequences of the decision. Now, the consequences of the decision, if I look at Rule 73 B or C, a request for certification, there are two things that the Defence must satisfy in order to get a certification. And that is, certification if the decision involves an issue that will significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. And then one more which says that in the opinion of the Trial Chamber an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. With respect to the first criteria, Mr. President, whether this issue will affect the fair conduct of the proceedings we say definitely yes, because if we use the Trial Chamber's ruling and what we understand of it as what is the meaning of good cause, that means that according to the standard, and the Trial Chamber has set the standard in its decision, pursuant to this standard it means that any future Prosecution requests will be considered in accordance with that standard. And that opens the door, in our view, with many more documents coming in, documents that were not on the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits, and on various criteria, but having a very low threshold as the Trial Chamber explained. Now when these documents come in, we believe this is both an impediment to a fair trial because as new documents come in, then it changes the case against the accused as we go along in the trial. That's for fairness. Now, as far as the expeditious conduct of the proceedings, if we go on with the Trial Chamber's decision, that means every time the Prosecution will apply for a new document, we already know that they will apply for at least three documents in relation to intercept one or the 20 April intercept. So already we know that we will have to file a -- an opposition to these three documents they will be requesting as a result, as a direct result of the Trial Chamber's decision. We also know that every time from now on and this trial is far from over, they will be applying many more times. My colleague has said, "We will continue to provide new intercepts." So as all this material comes in, every time we will have to file motions to oppose in order to protect the rights of our clients to a fair trial. This will indeed take much more time. Time on behalf of the parties, time on behalf of the Trial Chamber, time generally in this trial. This is for the first criterion. The second criterion is whether the Trial Chamber believes it may materially advance the proceedings in order that we can go on with this trial. Well, absolutely, Mr. President. If we get a confirmation by the Appeals Chamber that indeed good cause is, as the Trial Chamber has said, very low and allows the Prosecution to do what it wants when it wants, when it wants it and however it wants to do it, then of course we won't object every time after that. So we will save lots of time by going to the Appeals Chamber and getting a ruling. What is meant by good cause and what is the criteria? And as you know, Mr. President, we already have a standing or an outstanding request for certification on a similar decision that allowed new witnesses to be introduced and, again, new exhibits. So it has come to the point where we need to go to the Appeals Chamber to sort this out so that if we are wrong then of course we will stop objecting on this principle. But for now, we feel that we will continue to object every time there is a new witness, every time there is a new document, every time there is a procedure that is undertaken by the Prosecution which we feel is contrary to the rights and the interests of our client. So in order to solve all this, we feel that we absolutely meet both criteria under Rule 73 B, and that certification should be granted. Now, with respect to the second question that you invited me to address, which is whether Witness 77 should be allowed to begin or not with his testimony pending this application. Our submission is that Witness 77 should wait because if it is determined if certification is granted, and if certification is granted then we will go to the appeals and it might be that this document number 77, if the Appeals Chamber says that, no, it was not good cause, then the document -- or the intercept doesn't go in and there is no need for Witness 77 to testify. In any event, if he starts today he has to come back on Tuesday, and there is no -- not much sense in doing this when we know that maybe all of the testimony will be a useless procedure if that intercept goes out following our application. For all these -- these arguments and submissions, Mr. President, we simply ask you, one, to grant certification, and, number two, to wait until your decision is granted, whether this witness, that he can testify only once the matter has been resolved. As a last point, Mr. President, I'm not sure if my colleagues understood the -- your question about whether they would -- they are joining in or not to this application. Two of my colleagues have; I don't know about the others. My understanding is that they will join me in this motion for certification and that they will also join me in requesting that the witness be delayed until this matter is resolved. I would like this specific question put to each of my colleagues to see whether they yes or no, and so also I can know where I stand in this thing. I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. In addition to that, of course, it goes without saying, but also any of the Defence teams that wish to contribute to this debate, please do so by all means. And then I will revert back to Mr. Thayer. Let's start. Mr. Zivanovic has already intimated that he agrees. Do you wish to make further submissions to the ones made by your colleague, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would -- I fully back everything my learned friend Mr. Bourgon has said. I would just like to express one more time fear that the decision the way it has been adopted, gives an opportunity to the Prosecutor at the last minute before the witness arrives under pressure and when he needs to be heard urgently, would then provide some submissions that were prepared a month in advance while we are left with a day or two only to respond to such submissions. I would just like to add that, because it seems to me that that would be our chief motive to fully back this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But again, my invitation to you is to restrict submissions to the requirements under Rule 73 for the purposes of granting or denying certification. Mr. Meek has already associated himself. Do you wish to contribute any submissions yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Under Rule 73B I believe that the certification should take place. What I fear is that the important part is the significantly affecting the fairness of the trial, not the expeditious, but the fairness of the trial. I am really worried that this ruling is just going to turn into this trial being a trial by ambush. The OTP is going to be able to do whatever they want to, they're going to be able to bring in documents at the last moment like they have done here, and this where -- this is our problem. I fully agree with everything Mr. Bourgon has said, but I am very fearful this is going to turn into a trial by ambush case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams would like to make submissions? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of General Miletic does not adopt a position against the certification request because it is a document that does not concern our client, but since there is already a request formulated by a team of the Defence I would like to say that I support entirely the argument of Mr. Bourgon; that is that the witness should not be called to the bar until this problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour, more or less our position is the same as Ms. Fauveau. Basically it does not concern most our client, but as a matter of principle we do support what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I don't know if there are any further final submissions. None. None. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We, of course, oppose the motion for certification, as we did in a nearly identical motion for certification on the Trial Chamber's 6 December 2006 decision. The standard under 73 B has not been met under either prong. The good cause standard articulated by the Court today, we believe, is a strong gatekeeper and will continue to be, both when the Prosecution is presenting its case, as well as when the Defence is presenting its case. We expect that during this trial on both sides there will be similar situations and we believe that the good cause standard as articulated by the Court will more than adequately regulate the sort of fear that's been expressed here of floodgates opening and a trial getting out of hand, which simply, I would respectfully submit, that there is no record of in the past or predictor of in the future. We will continue to be very conservative and careful in presenting to the Court any future requests for additional witnesses or evidence. We trust the Court, as I said earlier, to continue to apply its careful discretion in balancing and actually, as the Court stated, prioritising the rights of the accused yet balancing that with the other realities and considerations of these complex trials, new evidence and the probative nature of new evidence and the other factors. Frankly, Your Honour, there is no record of ambush in this case. We have a record of a very complex case getting under way, and us dealing with the realities of preparing and prosecuting a very complex and a multi-defendant case. That is a far situation from ambush, that is a far situation from a Trial Chamber letting the Prosecution run amok. And as a member of the team, I can certainly represent to the Court that I don't feel like I'm being enable to run amok anywhere in this courtroom. I feel like we have conducted on this side as efficient as possible, given the circumstances, trial thus far. With respect to the specific provisions, Your Honours, of 73 B(ii), there is simply no evidence that this will efficient -- this will significantly affect the fair or expeditious conduct of this entire trial. This is a very limited issue. The Court has ruled on it in the past. The Court in the Prosecution's submission is applying a very limited and conservative standard, and again we will continue to work with all parties in terms of any future presentations we have to expand our witness list or our exhibit list. And we understand that the Court will continue to apply a case-by-case, carefully considered approach to any further requests. And there has been no showing, frankly, Your Honour, that there needs to be an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber that would materially affect these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may reply to the submissions of my colleague, with your permission. The only thing I will address is that my colleague has indicated that there were no indications that this trial was getting out of control and no -- no justification for the fear that we have expressed. Mr. President, since the beginning of this trial we started the trial, the Prosecution did not have a -- the case was not ready, we made submissions and we were turned down. The Prosecution has already applied for new witnesses in three different occasions. The Prosecution has already applied for new documents and I believe we are at the seventh submission of the Prosecution in this case. And every time the criteria that is -- appears to be used is indeed whether there was good cause and whether there is a prejudice to the Defence. Well, the prejudice to the Defence, Mr. President, is that when we prepared this case we were given a number of months to prepare this case and we have prepared this case. On the basis that what was announced by the Prosecution. And the case has to proceed on the basis of what the Prosecution put on its Rule 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits. We recognise that there are circumstances when an additional witness or when an additional document may have to come in, in the interests of justice. But what is happening now with the kind of criteria issued by the Trial Chamber today for good cause, it's not the exception, it's rather the exception will be that the Prosecution will not be able to introduce any kind of document. And for these reasons, Mr. President, we need to address this standard of good cause and this standard of whether or not the Prosecution can be allowed to continue in this type of proceedings. The case-by-case approach is not a right approach. It's a case-by-case if there is exceptionally a document or a witness that will change the nature of the case. But as far as the Defence we have prepared the case for the Defence, we are prepared each of our defences and now we are completely being kept off balance by new documents, new witnesses, and frankly, Mr. President, we don't know where the Prosecution is going with this case, although it should be, as it said, they said this was an obvious case, well it certainly does not look like an obvious case to us, the way they are trying, looking for additional and witnesses for issues such as this one. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that we have reached a stage where we can decide on your oral request for certification. As yet we need to discuss further. We have agreed to continue discussing this over the weekend. I'm sure you will be working over the weekend too, and we will come back to you with a decision or written on Monday -- on Tuesday, sorry. My apologies to you. In the meantime, we also feel that until at least we have decided the issue and how we are going to decide it we are not -- we don't know as yet, we will not start with the testimony of Witness number 77. I don't know his PW number. So, however, we -- simply because we don't know how we are going to decide this matter, it will be impractical on our part to give you instructions to return him home unless you feel that you can safely do that and have him returned in case we decide against the certification. As I said, we don't know where we stand on this, we will give it all due consideration it deserves, and if we are in a position to decide it on Tuesday, we will do so. In the meantime, Witness number 77 can wait. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, at the same level, again simply because we are still discussing and we need to discuss a lot more, if certification is granted there is also the possibility that Witness 77 will not start. So what I suggest is that while you retain 77 available, you also take necessary steps to have the subsequent witness available on -- on Tuesday, should we need to start with that other subsequent witness. All right. So that's the position, and you will work it out accordingly. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, regarding the witness that was supposed to be called after Witness 77, the Defence took note of your decision for the time granted for the cross-examination and we will indeed and obviously respect your decision, but I would like to ask you the following question regarding the witness that was supposed to be here on Tuesday. This is a person that was working as a crypto-protector. So the limits imposed for the cross-examination concern equally that particular person or does your decision concern only the operators who were intercepting telephone conversations? Because, in fact, if your limit is concerning as well cryptoprotection witnesses, I would like to ask you for more time with your leave because it is the only witness that can testify on crypto-protection and on the reports that were sent. We heard a few witnesses until now, but they were not able to tell us anything on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we seek a similar clarification. When Your Honour talked about MUP intercept operators, Your Honour include amongst them the SDB intercept operators? In short, are they one and the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our feeling was, you mentioned the MUP precisely because you yourself raised the issue, as you raised the SDB we probably would have addressed that as well. Mr. McCloskey had himself mentioned other possible future witnesses who were in a supervisory position. We did not address that. We will address that by -- on a case-by-case basis when it arises because one supervisor can be more important than another or one has less information to offer than another. But SDB, I would suggest that I give the floor to Mr. McCloskey to hear the OTP's position on this and we will come back to you on -- on this on -- on Tuesday. The same applies to you. You will understand, Madam Fauveau that this is something that requires consultation amongst us and that it will only be decided after due consultation has been concluded. But I thank you both for having made these observations, and I invite Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer, I don't know who wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, MUP means Ministry of Interior and CSB, SDB all those are Ministry of the Interior. So that's all the same. And just one reminder. Ms. Fauveau pointed out yesterday that one of our filings had mentioned there might be another witness that had done the same intercept as the witness I had. The -- then you brought the witness back in and he saw his handwriting. The mistake was in the filing. Just to let you know, we checked on that and she was correct. There is not another witness with the same intercept, and we are not claiming there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what happens to our decision then in relation to PW-137?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I have stated yesterday, I do not request that that witness be called back because the other intercept is really not important for my client. So because this question has been clarified, I do not need to have this witness called back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There are six other Defence teams and I don't know what their position will be. Anyway, we'll cross -- we'll deal with that when -- when ... So, I thank you all for all your constructive submissions and cooperation with the Trial Chamber. We will not be sitting on Monday, as already communicated to you, and on Tuesday we will start with our decision, hopefully, on the oral request for certification and move from there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
